p: In the year nineteen forty-nine, a German philosopher named Karl Jaspers, writing in the ruins of a Europe that had just destroyed itself, proposed a remarkable idea. He observed that in the space of a few centuries, roughly between eight hundred and two hundred years before Christ, and in several parts of the world that had little or no contact with one another, there appeared almost at once the thinkers whose ideas have governed the moral life of mankind ever since. In China, Confucius and Laozi. In India, the Buddha, the authors of the Upanishads, and the founder of the Jain religion. In Persia, perhaps, Zoroaster, though his date is very uncertain. In Israel, the great prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, and those who gathered the Hebrew scriptures in exile in Babylon. In Greece, the first philosophers, and then Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. Jaspers called this period the Axial Age, from the German word for an axis, because, he said, the history of the world turns upon it.

The Encyclopaedia reports, with proper scruple, that many scholars doubt the idea. The dates are too loose; the Hebrew prophets and Zoroaster do not fit neatly; the similarities between a Chinese moralist and a Greek metaphysician are perhaps more in the mind of the observer than in the evidence. Nevertheless, the idea has survived because it points to something real. Across the civilised world, in that period, men began to ask questions of a new kind. Not merely: how shall we please the gods so that the harvest may be good? But: what is a good life? What is justice? What is the self? Is there a law above the king? Why do we suffer? And they began to give answers that appealed not to custom or to power, but to reason, to conscience, and to an order of the world that stood above both.

Why it happened then is unknown. Some point to the spread of iron and of coined money, the growth of cities and of trade, and the rise of large states, all of which loosened the old bonds of clan and village and set individuals adrift in a wider and more dangerous world. When the old certainties fail, men look for new ones. That, at any rate, is the explanation I find most persuasive, and I note that our own century, which is likewise loosening every old bond, is likewise very fertile in philosophies, though I doubt that history will rank them so high.

Kong Qiu, whom we know by the Latin form of his title, Confucius, meaning Master Kong, lived from about five hundred and fifty-one to four hundred and seventy-nine years before Christ in the small state of Lu, in what is now Shandong in eastern China. It was a time of disorder, when the ancient royal house of Zhou had lost its power and its great vassals fought among themselves. Confucius was a minor official and a teacher, who spent years travelling from court to court in the hope that some ruler would employ him to put his ideas into practice. None did, for long. He died believing he had failed.

His teaching, recorded by his disciples in a collection of sayings called the Analects, is concerned above all with right conduct in human relationships: between ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, friend and friend. Its central virtue is a quality usually translated as humaneness or benevolence, the disposition to treat others as fully human. He taught that the ruler must govern by moral example rather than by punishment: if the ruler is good, the people will be good, as the grass bends before the wind. He laid great stress upon ritual and propriety, the proper forms of ceremony and courtesy, which he believed trained the heart as well as the manners. Asked once for a single word that might guide a man's whole life, he is said to have answered: reciprocity. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others.

After his death, his followers made his teaching the foundation of Chinese education and government. From the Han dynasty onward, for two thousand years, the officials of the Chinese empire were chosen, in principle, by examinations in the Confucian classics. It was the first civil service in the world to be recruited by merit, and our own reform of eighteen seventy, which at last requires examination for most posts in the government of this country, owes a good deal, through the example of the East India Company, to China.

At about the same time, in the valley of the Ganges in northern India, a young man of a noble family of the Shakya people, named Siddhartha Gautama, left his home, his wife and his infant son to seek an answer to the problem of suffering. The traditional dates of his life have been revised, and the Encyclopaedia now places his death, cautiously, around four hundred years before Christ. The legends say that he had been kept by his father in luxury, ignorant of the miseries of the world, until on excursions from the palace he saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering holy man, and resolved to discover the cause of all this suffering and its cure. For years he practised the severest self-denial, until he nearly starved; then, judging that this was no better than luxury, he took a middle way, and, sitting in meditation beneath a fig tree, attained what his followers call awakening. Buddha is a title, meaning the awakened one.

He taught for some forty-five years. His doctrine is summed up in what are called the Four Noble Truths: that life involves suffering, or dissatisfaction; that suffering arises from craving; that it can be ended by ending craving; and that there is a path to that end, the Eightfold Path of right understanding, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. He taught that nothing is permanent, not even the self, and that the goal of life is release from the endless round of rebirth, a state called nirvana, a word meaning blowing out, as of a flame.

Buddhism spread across India, and then, as Indian influence declined, into Ceylon, Burma, Siam, Tibet, China, Korea and Japan, and in the twentieth century, I am told, into Europe and America, where a great many people practise its methods of meditation without much attending to its doctrines. Of the founders of the world's great traditions, the Buddha is perhaps the one who would be least surprised by that.

These teachers did not agree. Confucius would have found the Buddha's renunciation of family a scandal; the Buddha would have thought Confucius too attached to the world. But they shared a conviction that was genuinely new: that a human being is responsible not only to his king and his clan but to a moral order that judges kings and clans alike. All later reformers, and all later rebels, have stood upon that ground.
